# Anaṅgaṇa Sutta (MN 5 (PTS MN i 24))

**ID:** MN 5 (PTS MN i 24)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Anaṅgaṇa Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 24  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta* (MN 5) is a discourse delivered by the Venerable Sāriputta in dialogue with Mahāmoggallāna on the nature of "blemishes" (*aṅgaṇa*), defined as the sway of evil, unwholesome wishes [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Rogell 2003]. The sutta examines four classes of individuals based on whether mental blemishes are present or absent and whether the practitioner accurately recognizes their own condition [Edo Shonin et al. 2015; Anālayo 2014]. Sāriputta emphasizes that honest awareness of one's defiled or undefiled state is critical for making an effort to emerge from defilements or nurture purity [Edo Shonin et al. 2015; Anālayo 2014]. This instruction is illustrated by the simile of a bronze utensil purchased at a market that is either soiled or clean and either tended and polished or neglected [Anālayo 2014]. The discourse also discusses those who go forth not out of faith but for a livelihood, characterizing them with terms such as *unnala* ("haughty" or "insolent") [Levman 2014]. At the conclusion, Moggallāna praises Sāriputta's teaching, comparing the joyful reception of the Dhamma to a youth placing a fresh garland of flowers upon their head [Piya Tan 2002; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anālayo 2014].

In later Theravāda exegetical literature, Buddhaghosa's commentary on the sutta (*Majjhimanikāye Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā*) is well known for citing an earlier verse from an unidentified source establishing the doctrine of two truths: conventional (*sammuti*) and ultimate (*paramattha*) [Ñāṇananda 1971; Walshe 1987; Levman 2014].

Curated full parallels in Chinese Āgamas comprise *Madhyama-āgama* MĀ 87, *Ekottarika-āgama* EĀ 25.6, and an individual translation, T 49 (*Qiuyu jing*, 求欲經) [Anālayo 2016]. Comparative analysis highlights minor variations across these versions: for instance, while MN 5 and EĀ 25.6 mention either a boy or a girl receiving the flower garland, MĀ 87 and T 49 mention only a woman [Anālayo 2016].

- Full parallels: EA 25.6 結; MA 87 穢品; T 49 求欲

**Sources**

- [Piya Tan 2002] Piyasilo Tan Beng Sin (Piya Tan), Buddha & His Disciples: Profiles and Perspectives in Self-Discovery (2002, 2004) — Details on the dialogue between Sāriputta and Moggallāna and the flower garland simile.
- [Edo Shonin et al. 2015] Edo Shonin, William Van Gordon, and Nirbhay N. Singh, eds., Buddhist Foundations of Mindfulness (2015) — Discussion of MN i 24 regarding discerning defiled and undefiled mental states.
- [Ñāṇananda 1971] Katukurunde Ñāṇananda, Concept and Reality in Early Buddhist Thought (1971) — Citation of Buddhaghosa's commentary to the sutta quoting the two truths verse.
- [Anālayo 2016] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Foundation History of the Nuns' Order (2016) — Comparison of the garland simile across MN 5 and its Chinese parallels (MĀ, EĀ, and T 49).
- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha (2003) — Context on Sāriputta's sermon inspired by Moggallāna on blemishes and evil wishes.
- [Levman 2014] Bryan Geoffrey Levman, Linguistic Ambiguities, the Transmissional Process, and the Earliest Recoverable Language of Buddhism (2014) — Notes on the term unnala in MN 5 and the commentary's two truths quotation.
- [Walshe 1987] Maurice Walshe, The Long Discourses of the Buddha: A Translation of the Dīgha Nikāya (1987) — Reference to the commentary on MN 5 quoting the two truths verse.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Title translation and thematic summary of MN 5.
- [Anālayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Perspectives on Satipaṭṭhāna (2014) — Analysis of the bronze dish simile and the garland simile in MN 5 and its parallels.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner’s Study Guide (2003) — Summary of Sāriputta's teaching on evil wishes and blemishes.
